utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I actually have a preliminary before he is brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have a preliminary. Then please raise it right away, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. On Saturday 1 November 2014, the Prosecution received an 18-page proofing note for the next witness. In this proofing note the Prosecution was informed that the Defence was redacting the entirety of 18 paragraphs and parts of nine other parts following the Prosecution's objections to the lack of foundation for the witness's knowledge of certain information in and absence of relevance. The Prosecution would like to put on the record that it maintains its position with respect to the remaining paragraphs as communicated in its response of 14 October 2014. The Prosecution further notes that the proofing note is essentially a new statement that goes beyond the matters opposed by the Prosecution. We would oppose the use or admission of the proofing note during the testimony of this witness. However, we do understand that the Defence may wish to lead additional evidence based on our previous objections to further establish the basis of knowledge for the witness's factual knowledge of the remaining paragraphs if relevant and not consisting of the witness's opinions. Because of this, we would not oppose this being done viva voce. However, we would be -- oppose it in the form of a proofing note which does now go into other matters, so like what the President of Argentina did and so forth. We would also note that the proofing note discloses information to the Prosecution based on the statement of another, and we also at this time have a significant inability related to this information which supposedly comes from another individual in another individual's statement. During the first recess today, the Defence did give us a copy of this other person's statement which is 56 pages long and not translated. This is rather difficult for us to -- to digest with such late notice. So I just want to put those matters on the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They are hereby on the record. Mr. Lukic, I must say that when I read in your new text lines like "from the media it become common knowledge that this and this happened," that, of course, is replacing one sweeping statement by another one and, of course, source of knowledge means that we have something more than what people read in newspapers. But again, it's maybe too much to -- to deal with right away. Let's see how your examination of the witness develops. And whenever decisions on whether or not to admit the old statement or the information report are still pending -- let's see how it develops, but I can't say that I have no understanding for the concerns expressed by the Prosecution. And that's true for the whole of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Mr. President, just if that ends the matter I'd just request to be excused if it's a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the usher is already at the door-step to escort you out, Mr. Traldi. And perhaps if he could then escort the witness into the courtroom at the same time, it would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Vlaski, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is handed out to. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Vlaski, you'll first be examined by Mr. Lukic. You'll find him to your left. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. But with your leave I would just shortly respond to the objections just heard from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Not in the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He does not speak English. If you want, he can remove his headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we would first have to establish that, that he doesn't speak any English. In view of his education I thought perhaps he might. But could we -- I think the Chamber is quite willing to hear, but I also said that after Mr. Weber expressed some concerns that the Chamber would see how it develops. Is there any way that we could start with the examination of the witness now and that you would further respond after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to know how to proceed, whether to go into details or just to offer the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There one simple basic rule, Mr. Lukic, and that is, ask for facts known to the witness. That's the reason why I gave this short quote, to ask a witness what happened. So clear source of knowledge, clear facts. That's what assists the Chamber. Is that clear enough guidance for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, that it will be -- become clear. I'm trying to find it in this proofing note as well what kind of source of information this gentleman used performing his duties, so I don't want to jump ahead. But also I would like to tell and emphasise that this 18-page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- information report is probably more than half is cut from the statement just for better understanding on which part of the statement the comments are directed to when there is more comments on one paragraph. So -- and we have -- I have with me six information reports offered by the Prosecution into the evidence. I have their numbers here if Your Honours want to hear them. This is -- this is not new in this trial, that we introduce information reports as -- as an evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm -- I'm not against it. Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- if you are not aware of the level of unsourced knowledge and opinion evidence -- let's not forget this is a witness of facts, and if I then read for these circumstances I can say that the fate of Yugoslavia was decided by, that's opinion. Again, I said we'll give you the benefit of waiting and see how it develops. And my guidance is facts, clear source of knowledge, and then we'll see what happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But if I may, Your Honour, only in that same paragraph you would find that he was actually providing security for one of those meetings he mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And does that mean that the fate of Yugoslavia was decided by. I mean, as a security detail you can't know what caused -- what was it that -- basis of the fate of Yugoslavia. These are general sweeping statements again. And even if you're there as security detail, that doesn't make an expert which could give these type of opinions. Again, you have the benefit of our doubt. I would say use it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Vlaski.

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For the record, could you please state your name and surname slowly.

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Nedjo Vlaski.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry, what is it that you have in front of you?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Just the statement that I signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please hand it over to the Prosecution so that they could take look at it and see that there's nothing else there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry, there is more in his hand, if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it appears to me to be a B/C/S copy of the proposed redacted statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, whenever you want to consult it, you should ask permission to do so. So you can have it nearby but if you put it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can manage without the statement. There's no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. It's available. If you need to consult, just tell us and explain why and then we'll decide on it. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Can we have on our screens 1D1768A. Actually, probably we have a problem with the system this morning. That's the hard copy we distributed to everybody in and around courtroom. So we'll probably have to continue with hard copy of this statement, Your Honours, so then the witness should have his hard copy with him at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the redacted version was already filed, so it must be in the system. We received it morning as a filing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I -- I was told that it's not in the system, so if it is, I would be happy to have it on our screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you assist in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not have the document in e-court. However, I can try and see if can I find the filing that Judge Fluegge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes it was attached to the filing. To that extent it should be somewhere in the system. If it's possible to show it on the screen, that would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I will do my best, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. For the time being, the witness can consult his version of the -- of his statement because I take it that you want the attestation --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you please take a copy of the statement which was returned to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please take your statement and I'm going to put questions to you that are based on the statement. Did you provide a statement to the Defence of General Mladic at a certain point in time?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Yes, I did give them a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the first page of the statement, do you see your signature?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: That is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the last page of your statement. And do you see a signature there?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Yes, I see a signature and the date of the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Whose signature is it and who put the date there?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Yes. This is my signature, and I wrote the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now we will look at the redacted statement. After it was redacted, are the contents of the statement accurate and truthful, according to your best recollection?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I was able to confirm. At the time when I gave the statement, everything was truthful and accurate and comported with the facts as I recalled them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions to you today, would you provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: I would give the same answers to some questions, and I would perhaps provide more detailed answers to some questions because I acquired more detailed information on those questions since I provided the original answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On Friday, Saturday, and Sunday, did you speak with me?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did we do on Friday, Saturday, and Sunday?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: We trimmed the statement that I gave during preparation. We redacted certain parts of the statement, and we provided certain clarifications in terms of the exhibits or proof that we had at our disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm going to put all these questions to you before I tender the statement and the information report. What kind of sources for your information did you used when you were carrying out your duties?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: According to the rules of operation of our service, all available sources --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the basis of the Prosecution's objections weren't necessarily what the generic general sources of information were but they're specific facts in the statement, and what we're looking for is what the witness's foundation is for those facts. Not some broad description of what an intelligence service has at its disposal. I just want to state that for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see that that is not your primary concern. At the same time, the Chamber would like the witness to answer the question, the generic question. Not to say that the problem has been resolved by that but we'd nevertheless would like to hear the answer of the witness. Could you please continue your answer. You were stopped when you said, "According to the rules of operation of our service, all available sources ..." Could you continue from there because we interrupted you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All available, formal, legal documents, public sources, all communications concerning persons of security interest were permitted and were the subject of the work of our service, including some specific methods and means the service uses, like gathering information through operatives, associates, gathering information through methods which perhaps violate secret private communications over the telephone, through carrying out illegal searches, following subjects, and all the other means that are at the disposal of a service such as mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. We've heard the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to put on the record that, in the meantime, Madam Registrar was able to put the document, the statement on the record, we see it in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It would hopefully help a lot with today's trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We would offer, Your Honour, both the statement and information report provided by this witness and having in mind that information report is confidential since there are some names mentioned this witness wants to protect, not to put them in any kind of danger. We'd offer both of those documents into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution does have objections I can rehash them. I've made them a record already. If -- I leave it to counsel's whether he wants to further remedy anything that we've made known as our objections during the course of their objections -- course of our objections. Otherwise, we're willing to have the material MFI'd at this point in time with the -- it being very clear that we made our objections known and counsel is having the opportunity to remedy them during their examination if they so wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Both documents will be MFI'd. Mr. Lukic, the report, the information report provisionally under seal, the fact that the witness wants to protect certain names doesn't mean that we are following that suggestion but for the time being it will be under seal. Madam Registrar, the numbers would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the redacted statement that has 65 ter number 1D1768A will receive exhibit number D735.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D735 is MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, the information report will receive number D736. However, I'm not clear on the number it will receive in e-court once it's uploaded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Number D736 is reserved for the information report which is confidential and once uploaded will be there. Mr. Lukic, just for your information, you asked for more guidance, and I said focus on facts and source of knowledge. I'll just allude to one example of your information statement. If I look at the comment to paragraph 43 of the statement, it reads: "This paragraph is self-explanatory." Yes? Now paragraph 43 is without any source of knowledge and gives almost exclusively opinion evidence and hardly any facts. Keep that in mind if you think that the matter has been resolved by your information report. And it's just one example that I give to you. And if you would read it, it's all opinion. But I'll let you -- please proceed as you consider appropriate. We'll later decide on admission of the statement. Also in view of how your examination-in-chief has developed and has clarified issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, in paragraph 8 of information report, we said that all information this witness gathered and presented in his statement is strictly work-related. So, in paragraph 43 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- he was part of that system and his job was to follow such a developments. He told me, if you want, you can ask him what he told me, actually, but it's obvious emanating from his work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if you read what remains from paragraph 43, "The legitimate interest and goals by the Serbian political representatives," that's opinion. Isn't it? Whether it's legitimate or not, what exactly their interest was is not explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These calls were without effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you read the whole statement, you would find what the Serbs were trying to protect: Their right to stay -- to have the same status they had before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Legitimate is an opinion, is a legal opinion, Mr. Lukic. And if at the same time you say they were subjected to various accusations and pressure, this was a case of tendentious depictions of the political and security situation wherein only the Serbian side was negatively portrayed, that's all opinion. If you are not aware of that, Mr. Lukic, you have a problem during your examination-in-chief, which you are now about to start. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will read a short statement summary of this witness, and then I will have a few questions for him.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Lukic provide the interpreters with a copy of the summary, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's in B/C/S. I can provide it to the interpreters, no problem, but I will need the help of the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if you only have the B/C/S version, would you please slowly read it, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After completing his education, he started his police career in the City Secretariat of the Interior, in Sarajevo on public security tasks. After a year, he was transferred to the State Security Service where he worked on all types of assignments, ranging from desk officer for operations equipment, inspector for security background checks, security of buildings and persons, inspector on internal affairs matters, and as chief of the SDB administration for security of persons and buildings. Mr. Vlaski began to work in 1975. Nedjo Vlaski will testify about the work of his service. He will testify about monitoring of all types of nationalism in the former Yugoslavia, as well as about the monitoring of the group Young Muslims, a group whose member was Alija Izetbegovic, as well as the monitoring of the trial conducted against this group in 1983 when the group's members were convicted to prison sentences on charges as a well-organised group that wanted to topple the constitutional system of the country and create an ethnically pure Bosnia and Herzegovina. He will talk about the surveillance of specific persons, including Alija Izetbegovic, after he was released from prison. Also, he will talk about the establishment of the Party of Democratic Action, the core of which was formed by members of the Young Muslims group and religious officials of the Islamic community of Bosnia. The witness will also speak about the actions of Alija Izetbegovic unrelated to any institutions and also about the influence of the Sura, the Islamic advisory council, on the functioning of the Party for Democratic Action and the actions of Alija Izetbegovic. Mr. Vlaski will also speak about the anti-constitutional activities of Muslim and Croat politicians of Bosnia and Herzegovina following elections which were held in 1990 aimed at the breakup of Yugoslavia. So this was the gist of the description of the tasks that were performed by Mr. Vlaski. He will also testify about the wire-tapping of Serb cadres and how it was conducted completely outside of the established system of institutional checks and balances. The witness will also talk about how Alija Izetbegovic managed to acquire almost complete control over all the sectors of the police. Nedjo Vlaski will testify about the division in the police of Bosnia and Herzegovina before the conflict broke out and about the links of Muslim politicians with criminals in Sarajevo before and after the conflict broke out. This intermingling of the Muslim leadership in the police and criminals created a favourable ground for the expulsion and killing of Serbs in Sarajevo. All of it began with the unpunished killing of Nikola Gardovic who was in a wedding party in the centre of Sarajevo whereby it was known who was the killer but the police did not do anything about it. This continued with the killing of Serbian policeman Pero Petrovic at the police station in Novo Sarajevo, who was killed in front of his colleagues, Muslims, by the Green Berets. This marked the open season on Serbs in Sarajevo. The witness will also explain the manner in which Muslim police officials armed Muslims and how they sent Muslim policemen for training in Croatia. That would be the summary for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. You have any further questions for the witness? Unless you would rather leave that until after the break and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I -- I can break now. It's a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then how much time would you need after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My plan was not to spend much time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- in leading this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll -- and what do you mean by "not much time"? Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I was deferring to your question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have to hear two audio recordings, and I might, during the break, find something from this informational report to go through with the witness. So probably 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. We'll take a break. We will -- yes, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, Your Honour. I just wanted to -- there is a number of objections the Prosecution did have and some of them were a foundational nature. I did communicate them to the Defence last week. If during the break if Mr. Lukic has any further information about those matters, dates, and when these documents were authored, things of that nature, I'd appreciate it just before I begin cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think the Chamber explained that it will usually not insist on -- on always to redact unsourced parts or -- et cetera but of course that the parties should be aware that if there are no sources given for the knowledge of the witness, then of course the probative value, if any at all, may not be -- may not be at a level the party presenting that evidence might expect or wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I may not have been clear. I was talking about the associated documents. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understood you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from that, I was briefly addressing Mr. Lukic as well who said that he would need some 15 minutes. We take a break and we will resume at 25 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, yes, first the witness should be escorted out of courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I just was reviewing the transcript over the break and I just -- it appears to me that there's been no 92 ter foundation established for D736 marked for identification, the information report. I just wanted to put that on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could you take care of that. Ask the witness to read the statement, not the information report which -- I don't know whether it's also available in the B/C/S or not. Is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll ask him. We -- I read him word by word the whole information report. We went word by word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We spent the whole Sunday on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but that's not the best basis for a --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All the Prosecution statements are read back to the witnesses before they sign it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But they're always also available in a language that witness can understand. Isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Provided later. If you want me, I can provide later to this with witness the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's -- we are now not talking about signatures on the statements. We are talking about admission into evidence and an attestation by the witness not before a signature but before admission under Rule 92 ter. That's a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I may, before the witness comes in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you can check it with the witness, if you wish so. Actually, this English version is made from the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay but --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Only not in this order and not this nicely put everything together, but first recorded what the witness told me, then I written this English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But that's all done outside of court. We cannot check in any way the accuracy of all that so, therefore, Mr. Lukic -- and since the witness now also cannot read the English version and since we most likely will not finish the testimony of the witness today, you might find a solution overnight for that and then present it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vlaski, again a question that has to do with this report. How did you and I go through this report?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: We went through it by analysing each and every paragraph in the statement, and then on the basis of the facts that were set out in the statement we provided a broader overview.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Yesterday, on Sunday, how did we go through this report that was written in English?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Well, we read the -- the statement and we looked at the evidence that I had. That is to say, augmenting all of this through the evidence that I had available to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that you have some documents. Before you started testifying, I came to see you during the break and I took three documents. Do you have more documents in your possession?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if we are still with the information report, this doesn't help. What we need to receive that report or the content of that report in evidence is either to elicit it viva voce, which would take hours, or to have it translated --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And to seek the attestation of the witness to that additional information. That's what we need. And there's -- how you produced it, et cetera, is -- well, may explain something but is not fit as the basis for admission into evidence. That's the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will abide by your guidance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vlaski, for example, if your working hours are from say, 8.00 a.m. until 4.00 p.m., if you hear some information that is of interest to your service, say, 10.00 or 11.00, or 3.00 in the morning, can you disregard that information?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: From an operative point of view, everything information that is of security interest has to be taken into account because this mosaic about somebody's activity is put together on the basis of this minute information that is gathered during the work of operatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During your work, was following the media a permissible source of information?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: In the rules of the security service, all the public sources of information available were one of the methods of collecting information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll ask you briefly --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, just before we get too far afield. There were changes in the rules of security service if I recall at different points in time. If we could just have some precision just about what time of work, what period the witness is referring to? Because he might have had some different assignments at different times?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How relevant is that? Whatever sources the office would gather, the issue is whether those sources of knowledge are sufficient for us. That's the issue. I mean, of course, you can read newspapers and whether you want to prepare reports on the basis of newspapers is fine. But, of course, what this Chamber has to do is to evaluate the evidence and to see what role newspapers - and I'm not saying none - but what role newspapers can play in our job to establish the facts. That's the issue rather than the issue you just touched upon. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you would receive some information through the media, what was the procedure that would follow?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Well, all information that is of security significance is compared to information that is obtained through other types of operative work. It is used as a kind of guide-line.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, my colleague from the other side, put a question. Could you be more specific in terms of when the media could be used as a source of information? You worked in a certain period of time before the war and then a different period of time after the war, and you were in the same line of work. Did anything change? Was anything banned in the meantime? Was anything done to disallow media?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Media are a very important source of information. They were used in two different ways, in a two-sided manner, because the media are a way in which both information and misinformation can be presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now let us go back to material sources. The documentation that was available to the State Security Service in Sarajevo, where is it today? Did it remain in Sarajevo or did you take it?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Well, there were several ways in which documentation was kept. Older documents were kept at the Zlatiste facility as far as I know because I was in charge of that facility when I was chief of the department for providing security for persons and buildings. That is where information from previous periods was stored. And then in different safety boxes in the State Security Service offices, other documents were stored. And then other documents, yet other documents were kept in the analysis department of the security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask you something. Can you tell us what remained in the hands of your service out of all of this, your service that remained in the territory that was under Muslim forces control?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: After military operations that ensued, some of these documents were taken and part of the documents that were under the territory -- on the territory of Republika Srpska authorities were kept there, whereas the documents that were kept in facilities that were under the control of the Muslim part of the area, that remained in their hands.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to speak slowly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're invited to speak more slowly. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And do pause before answering my question. Documentation that your service had, was it destroyed; and if so, did you take part in that?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: According to the rules of service, in certain periods of time documentation is destroyed. Just before the first multi-party elections were held, if I can put it that way, we had this thankless task to destroy part of the documentation there for political reasons and some other reasons; namely, that certain methods of work of the service and certain documentation in respect of certain individuals before the multi-party elections could be destroyed so that it would not be the subject of certain manipulations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A vast amount of this documentation was destroyed. I can say by way of illustration that I had three safes in my office and lots of these materials that did not really have much value and they were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For example, documentation that has to do with monitoring Young Muslims, where is that? What do you think? Do you think it's still there?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: I know that this part of the documentation was stored at the department for documents. Unfortunately, part of this documentation - that is to say, the part that is on microfilm - was taken away unlawfully by the chief of the State Security Service, Branko Kvesic, as he left the service and as he went from Sarajevo to Mostar to the area of Herceg-Bosna. Specific documentation about the activities of this group, the Young Muslims, was on those premises, and I had direct insight into that documentation before the multi-party elections were held. May I explain why I had this insight? I can continue, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave it to Mr. Lukic whether he puts questions to you in this respect. And, again, Mr. Lukic, general statements do not always help us very much. Rather, we'd like to know when the witness says A or B, why he knew about A or B.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You've heard what the Judge is interested in. Please tell us when this happened, if you know, and explain what it is that you wish to explain to us.

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: My superiors from the top of the security service, that is the period before the multi-party elections were held, gave me the task of looking into this documentation. On the basis of a cross-section that was supposed to be made, the leadership of the service planned to take certain measures of protection for operatives, inspectors, who did this work because some revengism was to be expected from the newly established authorities that, on the basis of our assessment, were supposed to come precisely from those circles that had been the subject of our operations beforehand. Let me say by way of information that out of a few members of the Presidency, Alija Izetbegovic was criminally prosecuted as well as Fikret Abdic, Franjo Boras, and in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Momcilo Krajisnik. I did review the entire files and documents that referred to the activities of The Young Muslims group who, headed by Alija Izetbegovic, were convicted in the trial held in 1983, and based on my review of those files, I had the opportunity to get to know numerous documents on that topic that were in the file. I submitted a report so that the service leadership could make a plan to protect the operatives, inspectors, who took part in certain measures, searches, informative interviews, investigations, or who were in any way would be possibly exposed as being part of these activities. I also know that a part of the documentation disappeared from the department for documents. This particularly applies to the dossier of Mr. Adil Zulfikarpasic who was a subject for many years of our work because he took part in the actions of the democratic alternative that was formed abroad for the purposes of working to change the system and the organs of power in the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us exactly how you found out that the dossier Zulfikarpasic disappeared?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: This happened quite early on because Adil Zulfikarpasic when he came to Yugoslavia tried to gain an access to that dossier through certain connections in the country. However, there was some compromising material from the dossier that was taken out of the file and passed on to Mr. Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, is there any way we could have some context as to when this occurred?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Lukic, apart from context, could you please put your questions in such a way that we do not get long stories which are, for us, not easy to link to what seems to be the core of this case and the core of the statement of the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm closing to the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you able to tell us when this happened?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: The disappearance of the file happened in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what is the source of your knowledge and do you know who actually participated in the taking away of this dossier?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: I do have some information. I don't have any proof though, so I do have operative information as is the practice in our part of the world, so it was information gained from sources that, based on operative knowledge, were able to access such information.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please not overlap and repeat the last two or three exchanges for purposes of interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you're overlapping with Mr. Lukic. You told us - and I invite you to resume from there - you told us that it was information gained from sources that, based on operative knowledge, were able to access such information. And could you please repeat what you said after that, unless Mr. Lukic's interruption was meant to stop the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Oh, no. It wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Could you please resume on from there, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These were our internal conversations by operatives who at that time were working in the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we go to the private session, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we now try to get an answer to the question. Could you tell us what facts are known to you which would shed any light on who were the ones who made that material disappear in 1991. So what facts do you know, even if you gained the information from operative sources?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, exactly, that's why we have to go to the private session. That's why he's reluctant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's move into private session for the time being.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this concludes my direct examination of this witness. And I don't know when we should deal with the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We're in a position to deal with them now and it might be useful to actually deal with them before cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Documents now being the Defence exhibits for Witness Vlaski. Let's go through them one by one. I think if I look at the list, it starts with non-associated exhibits you want to tender, or do you want to tender associated exhibits only?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Associated exhibit and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. The first one is the redacted signed statement and that's one that we have dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the second and the third on my list are P2984 and P2996 already in evidence. Which brings us to 1D03114, list of persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Objection based on relevance. There is no time or temporal context for this document and none has been established with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This witness can provide us with that details but it's obvious after the elections in 1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, that leaves still 24 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's only for the period after those elections. That -- how the power was distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And where in [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If it's not necessary -- [Overlapping speakers] ... sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Where in the statement did the witness comment on it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What paragraph? Because for associated exhibits, it's required that we can't understand the statement without the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid we might use too much time. Then my proposition to Your Honours is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- that the cross starts and I will prepare in which paragraphs this was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Weber, I take it that you'll have certainly some subjects in cross-examination which could you start before you -- before you -- we have dealt with all the associated exhibits. And, Mr. Lukic, would you carefully prepare the further submissions on the admission of the associated exhibits. By the way, Mr. Weber, I'm informed that -- well, that was a question by the Chamber, that it's paragraph 48 which deals with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 48, yes. Now I have the list with the paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have them all? Then we can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not all. Then we'll skip it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we'll ask Mr. Weber to start his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vlaski, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Weber. You'll find him to your right. Mr. Weber is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just to finish up on a -- well, good afternoon, Mr. Vlaski.

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Since we were talking about the conversations you had with the Defence over the weekend, I was just wondering yesterday, on Sunday, when -- in your decisions with the Defence, did you make any clarifications or corrections to information that you provided them on the days before, on Friday and Saturday.

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: We just shortened it and perhaps some arguments that could substantiate the facts that are mentioned in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Do I understand correctly from your answer that there were changes, then, that you made yesterday?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: There were no changes. It's just that certain parts of the opinions in the statement were made more specific in order to provide more details about the sources of information and to substantiate the number of documents that could back up the information. This is information that I -- I do have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, I'm afraid that we may not fully understand each other or the witness might not understand you fully. The issue raised by Mr. Weber is especially whether after you had talked on Friday and on Saturday with your Defence, whether in your discussions on Sunday anything was added or further explained or -- that is what Mr. Weber would like to know. Can you tell us whether in the continued conversation on Sunday anything changed what had you dealt with on Friday and Saturday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had a statement that I gave to the Defence team, the statement that contains a number of the evidence that would give an authentic form to my statement. So that is the statement that I provided to the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm not sure that we have clarified this. The precise issue that I'm asking this for is because I have been provided with information from the Defence that is dated the 1st of November, which is Saturday. I've not received information from the Defence after Saturday. So then I'm specifically asking you whether there -- during your conversations on Sunday, yesterday, were there changes?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: I did not add anything. All I wanted to do was to present the documents that I have in my possession. I have them in my room. So I wanted to present them in the sense that my attention was drawn to the fact that parts of the statement needed to be redacted so that it would gain evidentiary weight. So that was the thing that was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Was there anything to the Defence that you indicated that you needed to remove?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO VLASKI
utterances.text: I did not think that anything needed to be removed from my statement. I believe that that was my opinion, my position, about the events that I am testifying about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to leave it for now. Maybe tomorrow when the information report is uploaded I'd actually go into that a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I don't think it's clear to the witness quite what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry for interrupting, I think we were informed that the information is uploaded into the system.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's at least -- then we can everything on our screens -- well, if you have another few questions --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- we have three minutes -- more minutes to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I just wanted to also -- before we break for the day, I was wondering if I could ask you this afternoon or this evening before we come back tomorrow if you could look at the first remaining paragraphs before paragraph 96 and let us know tomorrow when we start whether or not everything you describe in those paragraphs occurred before April 1992. Do you understand that? You don't have to do it now. I'm not asking you to go through each paragraph right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What do you mean by the first remaining paragraphs before paragraph 96?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that everything that comes from 1 to 95?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Actually up to and including 96. And I belive now that -- there are some redacted paragraphs, so forgive me if I did not articulate that very well. But what I'm asking the witness to do is if there's any way he could review what's in the redacted statement from paragraphs 1 up to and including paragraph 96 and let us know tomorrow morning when we start if everything he is describing occurred before April 1992. And if not, to tell us what paragraph did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that clear to you? Mr. Vlaski, is that clear to you that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's clear to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- whether it all happened before April 1992 and if not to tell us tomorrow what events did take place either in April or after April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, with that being said I'm going to get into documents -- oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It seems from what I hear -- okay, it seems to be no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to get right into documents and it might take longer than where we're at right now, so if we can continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll then adjourn for the day. Mr. Vlaski -- Mr. Weber is invited to switch off his microphone. Yes, which he has done by now. Mr. Vlaski, before we adjourn I'd like to instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way, with whomever, about your testimony, whether that is testimony already given today, or anything about your conversations with the Defence over the last weekend, or whether that is about testimony still to be given tomorrow or perhaps even the day after tomorrow. If that's clear to you, you're invited to follow the usher, and we'd like to see you back at 9.30 tomorrow morning in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we adjourn, if the parties could in any way exchange the information about the associated exhibits to see whether there are any remaining questions or not so as to allow the Chamber to be focused tomorrow on what associated exhibits are in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- the Prosecution last Thursday provided a list with its objections on each exhibit and what they are and the ones that we don't object to. So we've received no further information since then. We'd, of course, appreciate any further information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid my friend is not completely accurate. We provided them with the audio recording he requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And -- Mr. Lukic is right. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That is a good end of the day. We adjourn and will resume tomorrow Tuesday, the 4th of November, and the parties are already made aware that Judge Fluegge tomorrow will be unable to continue to sit on this case, to hear the case for urgent personal reasons, and therefore, most likely only for one day, we'll sit 15 bis. We adjourn.
